section.title: A Penitent's Plea Under Chastening
section.sectionRationale: One of the traditional penitential psalms, David prays under the weight of sickness, sin, and abandonment by friends, while enemies close in. Its raw honesty about the body's collapse under guilt and the silence of a suffering man models how the Spirit teaches believers to bring confessed sin and physical affliction together before God.
section.thesis: David's body and soul collapse under the weight of unconfessed sin and surrounding enemies, yet even in silence before his accusers he confesses his iniquity honestly and waits for the LORD, his only Savior, to come quickly to help him.
section.frameNote: Four movements: the opening cry against God's disciplining anger, verses 1-8; the isolation of sickness, sin, and abandonment, verses 9-14; the psalmist's deliberate, hopeful silence before his accusers, verses 15-20; and the closing plea for God's quick and near help, verses 21-22.

units.label: O Lord, do not rebuke me in Your anger

verses.text: O LORD, do not rebuke me in Your anger or discipline me in Your wrath.
For Your arrows have pierced me deeply, and Your hand has pressed down on me.
There is no soundness in my body because of Your anger; there is no rest in my bones because of my sin.
For my iniquities have overwhelmed me; they are a burden too heavy to bear.
My wounds are foul and festering because of my sinful folly.
I am bent and brought low; all day long I go about mourning.
For my loins are full of burning pain, and no soundness remains in my body.
I am numb and badly crushed; I groan in {{naham|anguish}} of heart.

units.label: My beloved and friends shun my disease

verses.text: O Lord, my every desire is before You; my groaning is not hidden from You.
My heart pounds, my strength fails, and even the light of my eyes has faded.
My beloved and friends shun my disease, and my kinsmen stand at a distance.

Those who seek my life lay snares; those who wish me harm speak destruction, 
plotting deceit all day long.
But like a deaf man, I do not hear; and like a mute man, I do not open my mouth.
I am like a man who cannot hear, whose mouth offers no reply.

units.label: I wait for You, O Lord

verses.text: I wait for You, O LORD; You will answer, O Lord my God.
For I said, "Let them not gloat over me, those who taunt me when my foot slips."
For I am ready to fall, and my pain is ever with me.
Yes, I confess my {{avon|iniquity}}; I am troubled by my sin.
Many are my enemies without cause, and many hate me without reason.
Those who repay my good with evil attack me for pursuing the good.
Do not forsake me, O LORD; be not far from me, O my God.
Come quickly to help me, O Lord my Savior.

naham.gloss: A deep groaning or growling anguish, elsewhere used of the roar of a lion or the sea, describing a groan too visceral for words, wrung from the body itself.

avon.gloss: Iniquity, guilt, or the twisted, bent quality of sin, from a root meaning to bend or twist. David does not merely name his sin's acts but confesses its deep, distorting guilt.

basic.context: David prays as a man whose body and soul are collapsing under the weight of unconfessed and now confessed sin, while sickness makes him repulsive to friends and vulnerable to enemies who plot against him. Rather than defend himself, he chooses a deliberate, hopeful silence, waiting for the LORD alone to answer, and closes with an urgent plea for God, his only Savior, to come quickly.
basic.hermeneutics: One of the traditional penitential psalms, it should be read as a model of honest, embodied confession, sin and suffering are not neatly separated here, and its silence before accusers is not despair but a disciplined act of hope, trusting God rather than self-defense to bring the answer.
basic.originalLanguages: David's groaning is naham, a deep, visceral anguish, and his confession names avon, iniquity, the bent and twisted guilt of sin, not merely its outward acts. His silence, verses 13-14, is deliberate, choosing not to answer his accusers so that God alone might answer for him.
basic.typology: David's pattern of silence before accusers who plot destruction against him, choosing not to open his mouth in his own defense, anticipates Christ before His accusers, who also remained silent, entrusting Himself to the Father rather than defending Himself.
basic.christ: Jesus fulfills and transcends this psalm's pattern of silence before accusers: 'He was oppressed and afflicted, yet He did not open His mouth,' Isaiah 53:7, echoed at His trial, Matthew 27:12-14. Unlike David, Christ's silence was not for His own sin, since He had none, but bore the weight of others' sin, so that David's cry, 'Come quickly to help me, O Lord my Savior,' finds its answer in the One who is Himself that Savior.
basic.god: God is shown as both the disciplining Father whose hand presses down under sin's weight and the only Savior to whom the sufferer can finally turn, His discipline and His salvation are not opposites but flow from the same committed, covenant care.
basic.crossReferences: Isaiah 53:7 pictures the suffering servant silent before His accusers, as a lamb led to slaughter. Matthew 27:12-14 shows Jesus giving no answer to His accusers at trial. 1 John 1:9 promises that confessing our sins meets a faithful and just God who forgives and cleanses.
basic.oneStory: David's honest confession under the crushing weight of sin and surrounding enemies, and his hopeful silence waiting for God alone to answer, anticipates Christ, who bore that pattern perfectly, silent before His accusers though sinless, becoming Himself the Savior for whom David and every penitent sinner cries out.

context.literary:
Psalm 38 falls into three movements of unequal feeling, and the seams between them are marked by the names of God. Verses 1 to 8 are a body seen from inside: arrows, a pressing hand, bones without rest, wounds that rot, a back bent double. Almost every clause has God as the actor or the cause. Verses 9 to 14 turn outward to people, the friends who stand off, the enemies who set snares, and the sufferer who plays deaf and mute. Verses 15 to 22 turn upward again, first in trust, then in confession, then in a closing triple cry. The switch is signalled at verse 9, where the sufferer for the first time addresses God by the title Adonai, and again at verse 15, where both names sit side by side, 'O LORD ... O Lord my God.' The last line of the psalm, verse 22, ends on Adonai as well, so the psalm both opens and closes on the pair of names, with the distress in between.

The opening verse is a word for word copy of Psalm 6:1. That is a deliberate borrowing, or a shared stock of penitential speech, and it tells the reader what kind of prayer this is before the wounds are described. The psalm has 22 verses, the number of letters in the Hebrew alphabet, but it is not an acrostic; the count is worth noticing and no more. There is no Selah anywhere in it.

The centre of gravity is the pair of verses 13 and 14. They say the same thing twice, deaf man and mute man, a doubling that mimics the closed ears and closed mouth it describes. The verse that follows, verse 15, explains the silence: it is not resignation but waiting, and the reason given in verse 16 is that the sufferer wants God, not himself, to answer. The heading, in Hebrew a single word meaning roughly 'to bring to remembrance', also stands over Psalm 70, and it frames the whole psalm as a prayer that asks to be remembered.
context.historical:
The heading gives the psalm to David and calls it a prayer for remembrance, but it names no occasion, and the honest reader leaves the occasion open. What the psalm does supply is the social world of a sick man in ancient Israel. Serious illness was never only a medical event. It cut a person off. Skin disease under the Law meant living apart, torn clothes, a covered mouth and a cry of 'Unclean,' Leviticus 13:45-46, and even where no formal rule applied, the fear of contagion and the suspicion that the sufferer was under judgment made friends keep their distance. Verse 11 uses the very noun for a plague or stroke that Leviticus uses for a skin affliction, and the friends 'stand at a distance' the way the unclean were made to stand apart.

The same illness exposed the sufferer to predators. In a world without courts of appeal, a weakened man, and a king weakened by sickness most of all, invited those who wanted his place or his goods. Verse 12 speaks of snares and of speaking 'destruction,' a picture of whispered slander and plots that rise while the strong man is on his back. The enemies of verses 19 and 20 are the ones the psalmist has served, 'repay my good with evil.' A ruler who had done good and been rewarded with betrayal has a place in David's story, and the psalm fits equally well the season of Absalom's revolt, though the text never says so.

The theological setting is the covenant belief that God's hand governs sickness and health, Deuteronomy 32:39, and that His rebuke is a fatherly correction, Proverbs 3:11-12. That belief does not make the psalmist a case of simple cause and effect. It makes him a man who cannot tell where God's discipline ends and the ordinary decay of the body begins, and who takes both to God.
context.canonical:
Psalm 38 belongs to a small group of prayers that the church has long called penitential, Psalms 6, 32, 38, 51, 102, 130 and 143. Its first verse repeats Psalm 6:1 exactly, and its picture of a body wasting under God's displeasure is close to Psalm 6:2 and Psalm 31:10-11, where iniquity 'has drained my strength' and friends 'flee when they see me.' Set beside Psalm 32:3-5, it shows two sides of one experience. In Psalm 32 the sufferer keeps silent about his sin and his bones waste; in Psalm 38 he is silent before his accusers but not before God, and he confesses, verse 18. The cure Psalm 32 reports, 'You forgave the guilt of my sin,' is what Psalm 38 is still reaching for.

The psalm sits at the head of a run of prayers about speech and silence, and Psalm 39 picks up its theme at once: 'I remained silent,' Psalm 39:2, 9. Verse 19 is read in the New Testament as part of a family of texts about hatred without cause. The BSB footnote sends the reader to John 15:25, where Jesus says that the Law's word, 'They hated Me without reason,' is being fulfilled; the same words stand in Psalm 69:4 and are in the neighbourhood of Psalm 35:19. The psalmist's innocent enemies become the pattern for those who hate Christ.

Beyond the Psalter, the wound imagery reaches to Isaiah 1:5-6, where Israel is a body with 'no soundness,' and the suffering servant in Isaiah 53:7 is silent as the psalmist was. Hebrews 12:5-6 reads God's discipline as the mark of a Father who loves, and 1 John 1:9 gives the promise the psalm is waiting for: confession meets a God who is 'faithful and just to forgive.'

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The psalmist meant his hearers to see that a person can be right about God and still be in agony, and that the way through is neither denial nor despair. He does not defend himself against the charge of sin; he owns it, verse 18. He does not curse his enemies; he leaves them with God. What he does is lay everything out in the open before the one person who already sees it, verse 9, and then choose to wait.

Israel was meant to hear something practical in this. When sickness and sin are tangled together and no priest or counsellor can untangle them, the prayer of this psalm is still open. It is a model for worship in the hour when the worshipper feels God's hand as pressure rather than help. It is also a lesson in how to treat the accusers. The psalmist is deaf and mute on purpose, verses 13 and 14, because arguing back would put the matter in his own hands. He puts it in God's: 'You will answer,' verse 15. That is a confession of faith, not only a tactic, since the psalmist believes the only verdict that finally counts is the LORD's.

A third intention is the reminder that the closing words matter most. The last three lines ask God not to forsake him, not to be far, to come quickly, and to be his Savior. A reader who gets to the end of this psalm has been taught what to say when there is nothing else left to say.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The psalm describes one person's experience of sin, sickness and abandonment. It does not lay down a rule that every illness has a hidden sin behind it, and it does not command believers to hold their tongue in every quarrel. What it records is the way one man prayed. What it commands, by clear implication, is the pattern of that prayer: bring the whole self to God, name the sin, and wait for Him rather than for vindication from other people.

Care is needed with verse 3, 'because of Your anger ... because of my sin.' The psalmist himself draws the line from his sin to his suffering; the psalm does not draw it for anyone else. Other Scripture blocks the generalisation, Job 2:11-13 and John 9:1-3. It is equally unwise to swing to the opposite mistake and treat the psalm's link between guilt and pain as merely a superstition of an earlier age. A guilty conscience does hurt the body, and Psalm 32:3-4 says so in the same terms.

The silence of verses 13 and 14 is likewise descriptive. It is wise when a reply would be a bid to control the outcome, and it is not a command to stay quiet in the face of abuse or injustice. Elsewhere the Bible commands speech on behalf of the vulnerable, Proverbs 31:8-9. The psalm shows what one sufferer chose in one setting; Christian wisdom tests that choice by the rest of Scripture.

debates.question: Is the sickness of this psalm a punishment for a particular sin, or the ordinary suffering of a man who is also a sinner?

views.label: Direct discipline for a specific sin
views.case: Verses 1 to 3 speak of God's rebuke, wrath and hand, and verse 3 says 'because of my sin.' The vocabulary is the vocabulary of divine chastening, and verse 18 confesses the fault. On this view the psalm records a real case in which sin and sickness were joined by God's hand.

views.label: Ordinary affliction read through a guilty conscience
views.case: The psalmist never names the sin, and his enemies attack him 'without cause,' verse 19, which suggests he is innocent of what they charge. Some readers take the psalm as the voice of a sufferer whose sense of guilt is genuine but whose sickness may not have a single tracing cause. The general pattern of Job and of Jesus' word in John 9:3 warns against drawing a straight line.

debates.bearing: Both views keep the same practical instruction: when the conscience is troubled and the body is failing, take both to God without sorting them first. The psalm gives the sufferer permission to confess without claiming that every illness is a punishment.

debates.question: Whose voice is heard in the silence of verses 13 and 14?

views.label: David, in his own trial
views.case: The heading and the tone of confession place the psalm in David's own life. His silence is that of a king who will not argue with accusers while he is weak, and the plea to be answered in verse 15 is his.

views.label: The righteous sufferer, and so Christ
views.case: The New Testament does not quote verses 13 and 14 the way it quotes other psalms, but the psalm's pattern, a man hated without reason, silent before accusers, waiting on God, matches Isaiah 53:7 and the trial narratives. Many readers hear the psalm as a template that Jesus filled completely. The difficulty is the confession of verse 18, which Jesus could not make in His own name.

debates.bearing: The psalm is safest read as David's prayer that Jesus later fills out, not as words in Jesus' mouth. The link to Christ is by pattern of silence and by the stance of trust, and it needs the added thought that Jesus bore the sin the psalmist confessed.

study.originalLanguages:
Verse 2 uses one verb twice, and English hides it. God's arrows 'have pierced me deeply' and His hand 'has pressed down' are both from the verb meaning to descend, so that the arrows come down into him and the hand comes down on him. The same verb of coming down appears in the first line of each clause, giving the sense of a weight and a wound arriving from above. God is the one who descends, and in verse 2 the descent is in judgment.

In verse 3 the psalmist says 'there is no soundness in my body' and 'there is no rest in my bones.' The word for soundness, metom, appears again in verse 7 and in Isaiah 1:6, where a rebel nation is a body with 'no soundness, only wounds.' The word translated 'rest' in verse 3 is the ordinary word shalom, peace or wholeness. The psalmist is saying that he has lost both health and shalom, and that the loss reaches the bones, the frame that holds a person up.

Verse 4 says his iniquities have 'overwhelmed' him, in Hebrew literally 'passed over my head,' as floodwater passes over a man who cannot stand. Compare Psalm 69:2 and Psalm 124:4, where the same picture describes the waters. The image is then reversed in the same breath: iniquities are also a 'burden too heavy to bear.' Sin is at once water above and a load on the back. Verse 5 speaks of 'sinful folly,' from a root for the fool who acts without regard for God, which shows the psalmist locating the origin of his trouble in a lack of wisdom and not only in a lapse.

Verse 11 says friends stand aloof from his 'disease,' using nega, the noun for a stroke or plague, which is the standard word for the skin afflictions of Leviticus 13. Psalm 39:10, the very next psalm, prays 'Remove Your scourge from me' with the same noun. Verse 15 says 'I wait,' from yachal, the verb of hope that Psalm 39:7 also uses. And verse 20 says the enemies 'attack' him, from the root satan, to oppose or accuse, the root that gives the noun in Zechariah 3:1 for the accuser who stands at the right hand of the high priest. The psalmist's enemies have taken up the accuser's work against him.

typology.type: The sufferer stands apart from friends and kin, verse 11
typology.fulfillment: The psalmist's beloved and friends stand at a distance from his affliction, the way the unclean were kept outside the camp, Leviticus 13:46. In the passion of Jesus the disciples scatter, and 'all those who knew Jesus ... stood at a distance watching,' Luke 23:49. The correspondence is that a righteous sufferer bears his affliction alone. The escalation is that Jesus was Himself made a man from whom men hide their faces, Isaiah 53:3, and that He suffered outside the gate, Hebrews 13:12. The type falls short in one place: the psalmist was avoided because of his sickness and his sin, but Christ was abandoned though He had no sin.

typology.type: The silence of the accused, verses 13 and 14
typology.fulfillment: The psalmist plays the deaf and mute man, choosing not to answer his accusers. At His trial Jesus 'gave no answer, not even to a single charge,' Matthew 27:14, and Isaiah 53:7 had pictured the servant as a lamb that 'did not open His mouth.' Peter says Jesus 'entrusted Himself to Him who judges justly,' 1 Peter 2:23, which is the same stance as the psalmist's 'You will answer.' The escalation is that Christ's silence carried the sin of others, while the psalmist's silence came from a man who confessed sins of his own. The type also falls short because the psalmist waited to be cleared, while Christ waited to be raised.

typology.type: The one hated without cause, verse 19
typology.fulfillment: The psalmist's enemies are 'many' and hate 'without reason,' and the footnote to verse 19 points to John 15:25. There Jesus takes the same phrase from the Law and says it is being fulfilled in the hatred He is meeting. The psalmist is a pattern of the innocent hated by the guilty, whatever his other sins, and Jesus is the perfect case, hated without a shred of cause. The escalation is that the hatred which pursued the psalmist for his good deeds, verse 20, led Jesus to the cross. The psalm falls short of the fulfillment because David could only say he was hated 'without reason' relative to his enemies' charges, while Christ could say it without qualification.

study.christ:
The psalm leads to Christ by a pattern of silence, by a contrast in guilt, and by its final cry. On silence, the psalmist says he is 'like a deaf man' and 'like a mute man,' verses 13 and 14, and that he waits for God to answer for him, verse 15. When Jesus stands before the high priest and then Pilate, the Gospels record the same stance: 'Jesus remained silent and made no reply,' Mark 14:61, and 'gave no answer, not even to a single charge,' Matthew 27:14. Peter names the source of that calm: He 'entrusted Himself to Him who judges justly,' 1 Peter 2:23. What the psalmist chose in a crisis Jesus lived from first to last.

The contrast is where the psalm finds its depth. David is silent as a guilty man who has confessed, verse 18. Jesus is silent as the one on whom guilt was laid. The psalmist's opening words, 'do not rebuke me in Your anger,' are a prayer that God's displeasure would fall short of its full weight. On the cross that displeasure was not turned aside. Paul says 'God made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf,' 2 Corinthians 5:21, and Isaiah says 'He was pierced for our transgressions, He was crushed for our iniquities,' Isaiah 53:5. The arrows the psalmist felt in verse 2 have a target in the end, and the target is the Son, who bears in His body on the tree what the psalmist could only fear, 1 Peter 2:24.

The psalmist's body also has its counterpart. He speaks of wounds, of loins burning, of a heart that pounds and light that fades from the eyes, verses 5 to 10. Isaiah's servant is 'stricken by God, struck down and afflicted,' and 'by His stripes we are healed,' Isaiah 53:4-5. The healing the psalmist begs for through the whole psalm, and does not yet receive within its lines, is the healing that flows from Christ's wounds.

The last verse leads to Him by name. 'Come quickly to help me, O Lord my Savior' ends in a title the New Testament gives to Jesus, 'our Savior, Christ Jesus,' 2 Timothy 1:10. And John 15:25 shows Jesus Himself finding the pattern of verse 19 fulfilled in the hatred aimed at Him.

A caution is needed. Verse 18 is a confession Jesus cannot make in His own name, and the psalm cannot be read as though every line were on His lips. The safest path is to hear it as David's prayer that finds its answer in Jesus, who takes the sinner's place and gives the sinner His own standing, so that the man who cannot stand, verse 17, is 'in Christ Jesus' and free from condemnation, Romans 8:1.
study.god:
The God of Psalm 38 is a God whose hand is felt. The psalmist does not treat the pressure on his body as blind chance; he says 'Your arrows' and 'Your hand,' verse 2, and 'Your anger,' verse 3. The psalm assumes that nothing in the world of a believer's suffering lies outside the reach of God's rule. That is a hard truth, and the psalm does not soften it, but it is also a comfort in disguise, for if the arrows are God's the healing is His too. The one who wounds is the one who is asked for help. The same God appears in verse 21 with different words: 'Do not forsake me ... be not far from me.'

The psalm shows God as one who sees everything. 'My every desire is before You; my groaning is not hidden from You,' verse 9. The psalmist has no need to explain himself to God, and this shapes his prayer. He does not argue his case. He stops managing appearances with people and speaks to the One for whom nothing is hidden.

The psalm holds discipline and salvation together, and it teaches that they do not belong to different gods. Proverbs 3:11-12 and Hebrews 12:5-6 say the Lord disciplines the one He loves, and the psalmist stands within that frame even when he cannot feel it. His two closing titles, 'my God' and 'my Savior,' come from the same mouth as his cry about God's wrath. Wrath and rescue are both real, and both are aimed at bringing the sinner home.

God is also the one who answers. Verse 15 is a statement of faith in the future tense: 'You will answer.' The psalmist does not know when or how, and the psalm ends with an unanswered plea, yet he leans his weight on the character of the God who has revealed Himself as slow to anger and abounding in loving devotion, Exodus 34:6. God's nearness is the thing he lacks and begs for. That he asks for it at all shows he believes God can be near even to a man in his condition.

For worship, the psalm teaches that confession is safe before this God. To say 'I confess my iniquity' is not to invite a fresh blow but to step into the promise of 1 John 1:9. It also teaches that our prayers may be short and raw. God receives a groan as a real prayer, and He takes it, in the words of verse 9, as something already before Him.

crossReferences.note: Verse 1 of Psalm 38 is word for word Psalm 6:1. Both psalms ask that God's rebuke not be given in anger, both describe bones in agony, and Psalm 6 adds the cry 'How long, O LORD, how long?' The two are companion prayers of a sufferer who believes God is the source of the pain and the only hope of relief.

The other side of the same experience. There the sinner keeps silent about his guilt and his bones become brittle, 'Your hand was heavy upon me,' and the release comes when he acknowledges his sin and is forgiven. Psalm 38:18 is the confession Psalm 32 tells us leads to relief.

A near neighbour in imagery: iniquity has drained strength, bones waste away, and friends flee at the sight. Comparing it with Psalm 38:10-11 shows how common the pattern of illness, isolation and guilt was in Israel's praying, and how the psalmists used the same words to bring it to God.

Isaiah describes rebellious Israel as a body with 'no soundness,' wounds and festering sores 'neither cleansed nor bandaged.' The words echo Psalm 38:3 and 38:5. The psalmist's private suffering thus becomes a picture of the whole nation's condition under sin, and of how much healing it needs.

The law of the person with a skin affliction, who must live alone outside the camp. Psalm 38:11 uses the same noun for the psalmist's 'disease' and describes friends standing at a distance. The psalm shows the human cost of separation the Law laid down, and prepares us for the One who touched the unclean.

The servant 'did not open His mouth,' led 'like a lamb to the slaughter.' The psalmist's deaf and mute silence in verses 13 and 14 belongs to the same family of faith. Isaiah takes the stance of the righteous sufferer and shows it in one who carries the sins of others.

Jesus says the Law's word 'They hated Me without reason' is being fulfilled. The footnote at Psalm 38:19 sends readers here. The psalmist's experience of being hated 'without cause' becomes a pattern that comes to its fullest case in Christ, with the note that Jesus applies it to Himself without any admission of guilt.

Peter says that when Jesus was abused He 'did not retaliate' and 'entrusted Himself to Him who judges justly.' The phrase names the inner stance behind the psalmist's silence. It is the apostolic reading of what it means to wait on God to answer rather than answer for oneself.

The writer recalls the word of Proverbs 3 that 'the Lord disciplines the one He loves.' It reframes the God's-hand language of Psalm 38:1-2 for the believer: what feels like arrows may be a father's correction, aimed at holiness, and it is a mark of sonship rather than a sign of rejection.

'If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us.' The psalmist says 'I confess my iniquity' in verse 18 without yet hearing the answer. John states the answer in advance for every believer: confession meets forgiveness and cleansing because God is both faithful and just, not despite His justice.

The next psalm takes up the theme of silence and discipline: 'I do not open my mouth because of what You have done,' and 'Remove Your scourge from me,' using the same noun as Psalm 38:11. The pair reads as two stages of one experience of learning to be quiet under God's hand and to ask for mercy.

'If You, O LORD, kept track of iniquities, then who could stand? But with You there is forgiveness.' The psalmist of 38 says his iniquities are too heavy to bear, and the psalmist of 130 says why the burden can be lifted. It supplies the theology behind the confession of verse 18.

study.oneStory:
Psalm 38 answers a question that Genesis 3 leaves hanging over every human life: what does it feel like to live in a world that has fallen, in a body that is failing, among people who cannot or will not help? The sickness of the psalm is not a private accident. It belongs to the world after Eden, where the ground is cursed, Genesis 3:17-19, and the body returns to dust. The shame and the hiding of Genesis 3:7-10 are there too, in the friends who keep away and in the sufferer who says he is bent and brought low.

Its confession also sits in the middle of the story of covenant. God has said He is 'slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness,' Exodus 34:6, and He has given Israel a system of sacrifice by which sinners may draw near. Yet the psalmist has no lamb in the psalm. He has only his groaning and his honest word, and he leans on the promise that God will answer. That is the situation of Israel again and again in the Old Testament, in exile and out of it: a people who know they have sinned, with little to bring but a confession and a hope.

The psalm sets up what comes next. Psalm 39 continues the silence, Psalm 40 recalls a rescue from the pit and a new song, and Psalm 41 ends the book with betrayal and blessing. The wider plot of the Bible then supplies the answer the psalm cannot give in its own lines. The sufferer who is hated without cause and silent before accusers is met by a Savior who is hated without cause, silent before accusers, and pierced for the iniquities the psalmist confesses. In Christ the arrow finds its true mark and the burden is carried away.

The new creation is the end of everything this psalm laments. There will be 'no more death or mourning or crying or pain,' Revelation 21:4. The body that could find no soundness is made whole, Philippians 3:21, and the God who seemed far is near, for He 'will dwell with them,' Revelation 21:3. The final line of the psalm, 'Come quickly,' is taken up at the end of the Bible in the church's own prayer, 'Come, Lord Jesus,' Revelation 22:20.

quiz.q: How does David describe the effect of his sin on his body in verses 3-8?

options.text: His body has collapsed under the weight, no soundness in his bones, festering wounds, burning pain, and groaning anguish.
options.note: David draws a vivid, visceral picture of sin's physical toll, not merely a spiritual or emotional struggle.

options.text: He reports feeling entirely unaffected physically by his sin.
options.note: The passage describes intense physical suffering directly connected to his sin and God's discipline.

options.text: He describes only a mild, passing discomfort.
options.note: The language used, overwhelmed, too heavy to bear, festering, crushed, describes severe and prolonged suffering, not mild discomfort.

options.text: He blames his friends entirely for his physical condition.
options.note: David attributes his condition to his own sin and God's discipline in verses 3-5, not to his friends, who are addressed separately in verse 11.

quiz.q: How do David's friends and kinsmen respond to his condition in verse 11?

options.text: His beloved and friends shun his disease, and his kinsmen stand at a distance.
options.note: This verse explicitly describes relational abandonment compounding his physical and spiritual suffering.

options.text: They gather around him with constant support and comfort.
options.note: The text explicitly describes abandonment and distance, not gathered support.

options.text: They join his enemies in actively plotting against him.
options.note: The text distinguishes passive withdrawal by friends, verse 11, from active plotting by enemies, verse 12.

options.text: They are unaware of his condition entirely.
options.note: The text implies they are aware but choose to withdraw and keep their distance, not that they are ignorant of his state.

quiz.q: What does David deliberately choose to do in the face of his accusers, verses 13-14?

options.text: He remains silent, like a deaf man who does not hear and a mute man who does not answer.
options.note: This deliberate silence, choosing not to defend himself, anticipates Christ's silence before His own accusers.

options.text: He launches an aggressive public defense against every accusation.
options.note: The text explicitly describes silence, not vigorous self-defense.

options.text: He asks his friends to speak on his behalf.
options.note: His friends have already withdrawn, verse 11, and the text describes his own personal silence, not delegated defense.

options.text: He curses his enemies openly.
options.note: The text describes restrained silence rather than open cursing or confrontation.

quiz.q: What does David explicitly do in verse 18?

options.text: He confesses his iniquity and is troubled by his sin.
options.note: This direct confession is the psalm's turning point toward hope, echoed in 1 John 1:9's promise of forgiveness for confessed sin.

options.text: He denies having done anything wrong.
options.note: The text is an explicit confession, the opposite of denial.

options.text: He blames his enemies for his own sin.
options.note: The confession is personal and direct, 'I confess my iniquity,' not a transfer of blame to enemies.

options.text: He asks God to forget that sin ever occurred without acknowledging it himself.
options.note: The verse is an active, personal confession, not merely a request for God to overlook sin unacknowledged.

quiz.q: How does this psalm's pattern of silent suffering before accusers anticipate Christ?

options.text: Jesus, though sinless, was also silent before His accusers, fulfilling Isaiah 53:7 and Matthew 27:12-14.
options.note: David's silence flowed from his own guilt; Christ's silent suffering, though sinless, bore the guilt of others.

options.text: Jesus loudly defended Himself at every stage of His trial.
options.note: The Gospels explicitly describe Jesus giving no answer to His accusers, fulfilling the pattern of silence, not loud self-defense.

options.text: Jesus is never described as silent anywhere in the Gospels.
options.note: Matthew 27:12-14 explicitly records Jesus's silence before His accusers.

options.text: This psalm has no meaningful connection to Christ's suffering.
options.note: The psalm's pattern of confession, isolation, and silent suffering closely anticipates the suffering servant of Isaiah 53 and Christ's own trial.

questions: David describes his sin's effect on his very body, not just his conscience. Where have you experienced the physical or emotional toll of unconfessed sin, and what changed when you finally brought it honestly before God?
David's friends withdrew from him in his affliction. Have you ever been the one withdrawing from a suffering friend, or the one left alone? How does this psalm shape compassion for both positions?
David chooses deliberate silence before his accusers rather than self-defense, trusting God to answer for him. Where are you tempted to defend yourself rather than entrust your reputation to God?
Verse 18 is a direct, undefended confession, 'I confess my iniquity.' What sin are you currently minimizing, excusing, or avoiding naming plainly before God?
The psalm ends urgently, 'Come quickly to help me, O Lord my Savior.' Where in your life right now do you most need to pray those exact words?

translationNotes.note: Anguish renders naham, a deep groaning elsewhere used of a lion's roar or the sea's roar, describing a groan wrung from the body rather than mere sadness.
Iniquity renders avon, from a root meaning to bend or twist, naming sin's distorting guilt rather than only its outward acts.
The comparisons to a deaf and mute man describe David's deliberate choice not to answer his accusers, not an actual physical inability to hear or speak.
